module_title: Tools, Materials, and Safety for Grafting

lessons.title: Selecting the right grafting knife and sharpening it like a pro
lessons.body:
A grafting knife is your most important tool. You need a knife with a straight, thin blade made of high-carbon steel. Avoid stainless steelâit dulls faster. In African markets, look for knives made in Kenya, Tanzania, or imported from Japan. Expect to pay 1,500â4,000 KES (10â30 USD). The best blade is 7â10 cm long, 1.5â2 mm thick, and has a single bevel (flat on one side, angled on the other). This lets you make clean, flat cuts. A folding knife with a locking blade is safer to carry. Some grafters use a utility knife with replaceable blades, but they are not as precise. If you cannot find a grafting knife, a sharp pocket knife or a new razor blade held in a wooden handle can work for small stems.

Sharpening is critical. A dull knife crushes plant tissue, and the graft fails. You need a sharpening stone (whetstone) with two grits: coarse (around 400 grit) and fine (1000â3000 grit). Lubricate with water or vegetable oil. Hold the knife at a 15â20 degree angle against the stone. Push the blade forward as if slicing the stone. Do 10 strokes on one side, then 10 on the other. Repeat with the fine grit. Finally, strop on a piece of leather or cardboard to remove the burr. Test sharpness by slicing a ripe tomato or a piece of paperâit should cut cleanly without tearing.

Sharpen your knife every day you graft, or after every 30â40 cuts. Keep a small stone in your kit. Never use a grinderâit overheats the steel and ruins the temper. Store the knife in a sheath or a wooden block. A well-maintained knife can last 5â10 years. If the blade gets nicked, grind it down on the coarse stone until the edge is smooth again. Remember: a sharp knife is safer than a dull one because it requires less force and is less likely to slip.

lessons.title: Making a simple grafting tool kit from locally available materials
lessons.body:
You do not need expensive tools to start grafting. With a few locally available items, you can build a complete kit for under 2,000 KES (15 USD). The core items are: a grafting knife (see Lesson 1), a pruning shear, a small saw, a sharpening stone, grafting tape, and a disinfectant. You can also add a flat file, a pair of pliers, and a roll of plastic strips cut from old polythene bags.

For a pruning shear, buy a good-quality bypass shear from a local agrovet. Expect to pay 800â1,500 KES. Avoid anvil shearsâthey crush stems. A small folding saw (like a pruning saw) costs 500â1,000 KES and is useful for thicker branches. If you cannot afford a saw, a machete or a sharp panga can work, but be careful. For a sharpening stone, a combination whetstone (coarse and fine) costs 300â600 KES. You can also use a smooth river stone and a piece of fine sandpaper glued to a flat board.

For grafting tape, you can cut strips from a clean, strong polythene bag (the type used for shopping). Cut strips 1â2 cm wide and 20â30 cm long. Alternatively, use paraffin film (Parafilm) if available, or rubber bands cut from old inner tubes. For wax, you can melt beeswax or candle wax mixed with a little vegetable oil. For disinfectant, use methylated spirit (denatured alcohol) or a 10% bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water). Keep everything in a small wooden box or a cloth bag with pockets. Label each item. A well-organised kit saves time and prevents injuries. Make a checklist and replace items as they wear out.

lessons.title: Sourcing grafting tape, wax, and disinfectants in African markets
lessons.body:
In most African countries, you can find grafting supplies in larger agrovet shops, horticultural supply stores, or open-air markets that sell farm inputs. In Kenya, for example, visit Kariobangi or Wakulima market in Nairobi, or agrovets in Nakuru and Eldoret. In Tanzania, check Kariakoo market in Dar es Salaam. In Uganda, look in Nakasero market or Kampalaâs industrial area. Prices vary: a roll of Parafilm (2.5 cm wide, 30 m long) costs 1,000â2,000 KES. Grafting wax (500 g) costs 500â1,000 KES. Methylated spirit (1 litre) costs 300â500 KES. Bleach (1 litre) costs 100â200 KES.

If you cannot find commercial grafting tape, make your own. Cut strips from clear polythene bags (the ones used for packaging). Avoid black plasticâit overheats the graft. For wax, you can use beeswax from local beekeepers, mixed with 20% vegetable oil to keep it soft. Some farmers use candle wax or paraffin wax. For disinfectant, methylated spirit is best. If unavailable, use a strong solution of potassium permanganate (purple crystals) dissolved in water until it is deep pink. Or use a 10% bleach solution, but rinse tools with clean water after to prevent corrosion.

Buy in bulk to save money. Split a roll of tape with other farmers. Store tape and wax in a cool, dark placeâheat makes tape sticky and wax soft. Disinfectants should be kept in tightly closed bottles, away from children. Always check expiry dates. If you are in a remote area, ask your local agricultural extension officer for sources. Many projects (like those funded by NGOs) distribute free or subsidised supplies. Join a farmer group to pool orders and get better prices.

lessons.title: Safe handling of sharp tools and preventing infection
lessons.body:
Grafting involves sharp tools, and cuts are common. The first rule is: always cut away from your body. Never hold the wood in your hand while cuttingâplace it on a firm surface or use a cutting board. Keep your fingers behind the blade. When using a knife, make slow, controlled strokes. Do not rush. If you are tired, take a break. Most accidents happen when people are distracted or in a hurry.

Wear protective gloves. Leather gloves are best for handling thorny branches, but they reduce feel. For fine grafting, you can wear tight-fitting rubber gloves or none at all, but be extra careful. Always wear closed shoesâa dropped knife can cut your foot. Safety glasses are recommended when sharpening or cutting dry wood, as chips can fly. Keep your tools sharp; a dull knife requires more force and can slip. Store knives in sheaths when not in use. Never leave a knife on the ground or on a bench where someone might brush against it.

Infection control is also about the plant. Dirty tools can spread viruses, bacteria, and fungi from one tree to another. Before you start grafting, wipe your knife and shears with methylated spirit or a 10% bleach solution. Dip the blade in the disinfectant for 30 seconds, then let it air-dry. Do this between every tree, especially if you are working with sick plants. If you cut into a diseased branch, sterilise immediately. For the grafter, clean any cut with soap and water, apply an antiseptic, and cover with a plaster. If you get a deep cut, seek medical help. Tetanus shots are recommended if you work with soil and plants regularly. Keep a small first-aid kit in your grafting box: plasters, antiseptic cream, and clean cloth.

lessons.title: Building a cheap grafting bench or working table
lessons.body:
A grafting bench gives you a stable, clean surface to work on. It saves your back and makes precise cuts easier. You can build one from locally available materials for under 3,000 KES (20 USD). The simplest design is a wooden table 90 cm high, 60 cm deep, and 120 cm wide. Use treated timber (e.g., 2x4 inch or 5x10 cm) for the legs and frame. The top can be a piece of plywood (18 mm thick) or planks nailed together and sanded smooth. If you cannot afford plywood, use a large wooden crate or a flat door. Make sure the top is level and free of splinters.

Add a vice or a clamp to hold the rootstock. A small woodworking vice costs 1,500â2,500 KES. Alternatively, use a C-clamp (500 KES) to hold a piece of wood that acts as a stop. You can also nail two wooden blocks to the table to create a V-shaped cradle for holding branches. For a cutting surface, place a plastic cutting board (200 KES) on the table. This protects the table and is easy to disinfect. Attach a small shelf underneath for your tools. Add a hook on the side for your pruning shear.

If you have no space for a permanent bench, make a portable one. Use a sturdy wooden box (like a tomato crate) turned upside down. Or use a folding table. You can also work on a tree stumpâjust make sure it is flat and clean. Whatever you use, keep it clean. Wipe it down with disinfectant before and after each grafting session. Do not let soil or plant debris accumulate. A clean bench reduces the risk of infection. If you graft many trees, consider building a simple shade structure over the bench to protect you and the grafts from direct sun and rain.

lessons.title: Daily maintenance and storage of grafting equipment
lessons.body:
At the end of each grafting day, spend 10 minutes maintaining your tools. This keeps them sharp, safe, and ready for the next use. Start with the knife. Wipe the blade with a cloth to remove sap and dirt. If sap is sticky, use a little methylated spirit or vegetable oil. Then dry it. Check the edge for nicks or dullness. If dull, give it a few strokes on the fine stone and strop. Apply a thin coat of oil (cooking oil or machine oil) to prevent rust. Do not store the knife wet. Put it back in its sheath.

Clean your pruning shear and saw. Remove sap and debris with a wire brush or a rag. Oil the pivot point of the shear with a few drops of oil. Check the blade for tightnessâif loose, tighten the nut. Replace worn blades. For the saw, brush off sawdust and apply a little oil to the blade. Clean your sharpening stone with water and a brush; do not use soap. Let it dry before storing.

Store all tools in a dry place, away from moisture. A wooden box with a lid is ideal. If you use a cloth bag, hang it on a wall. Never leave tools on the groundâmoisture causes rust and you might step on them. Keep disinfectants in a separate, closed container. Grafting tape and wax should be stored in a cool, dark place. If you have leftover tape, wrap it in a plastic bag to keep it clean. Make a daily checklist: knife sharpened? tools cleaned? disinfectant refilled? This habit will make your tools last for years. Replace any broken or worn-out tools immediately. A well-maintained kit is a sign of a professional grafter.

quiz.q: What is the best blade material for a grafting knife?
quiz.explanation: High-carbon steel holds a sharper edge longer than stainless steel.

quiz.q: What angle should you hold the knife against the sharpening stone?
quiz.explanation: A 15â20 degree angle produces a sharp, durable edge for grafting.

quiz.q: How often should you sharpen your grafting knife?
quiz.explanation: Daily sharpening keeps the knife effective and safe.

quiz.q: Which type of pruning shear is recommended for grafting?
quiz.explanation: Bypass shears make clean cuts without crushing stems.

quiz.q: What can you use as a cheap alternative to grafting tape?
quiz.explanation: Polythene strips are flexible, cheap, and widely available.

quiz.q: What is a good disinfectant for grafting tools?
quiz.explanation: Methylated spirit kills pathogens without corroding tools.

quiz.q: How should you store grafting tape?
options: B) In a cool, dark place
quiz.explanation: Heat makes tape sticky; cool, dark storage preserves it.

quiz.q: What is the first rule of safe tool handling?
options: B) Cut away from your body
C) Hold wood in your hand
quiz.explanation: Cutting away from your body reduces the risk of injury.

quiz.q: Why should you disinfect tools between trees?
quiz.explanation: Disinfecting prevents transmission of viruses and fungi.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get a deep cut while grafting?
options: B) Wash and apply a plaster
quiz.explanation: Deep cuts need professional medical attention to prevent infection.

quiz.q: What is a cheap material for a grafting bench top?
quiz.explanation: Plywood is affordable, smooth, and easy to work with.

quiz.q: What can you use to hold rootstock on a bench?
quiz.explanation: A C-clamp securely holds wood in place for cutting.

quiz.q: How often should you clean your grafting bench?
options: B) Before and after each session
quiz.explanation: Cleaning before and after prevents infection and keeps the surface safe.

quiz.q: What oil can you use to prevent rust on tools?
quiz.explanation: Cooking oil is a cheap, effective rust preventive.

quiz.q: Where should you store grafting tools?
quiz.explanation: A dry box protects tools from moisture and rust.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a professional grafter?
quiz.explanation: A well-maintained kit shows care and competence.

quiz.q: What is the best way to test if a knife is sharp?
quiz.explanation: A sharp knife slices a tomato cleanly without crushing.

quiz.q: What should you do if your knife gets a nick?
options: B) Grind it down on a coarse stone
quiz.explanation: Grinding on a coarse stone removes the nick and restores the edge.

quiz.q: What is a good alternative to a commercial grafting wax?
quiz.explanation: Beeswax with oil is a traditional, effective grafting seal.

quiz.q: Where can you often find grafting supplies in African cities?
quiz.explanation: Agrovet shops specialise in farm inputs and tools.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid black plastic for grafting tape?
quiz.explanation: Black plastic absorbs heat and can kill the graft.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of buying supplies in bulk?
quiz.explanation: Bulk buying reduces the cost per item.

quiz.q: What should you wear when grafting thorny branches?
quiz.explanation: Leather gloves protect hands from thorns and cuts.

quiz.q: What is a good first-aid item for a grafting kit?
quiz.explanation: Plasters are essential for treating minor cuts.

quiz.q: What is a portable alternative to a grafting bench?
quiz.explanation: A flat tree stump can serve as a makeshift bench.

quiz.q: How should you clean a sharpening stone?
options: B) With water and a brush
quiz.explanation: Soap can clog the stone; water and a brush are best.

quiz.q: What should you do with a dull pruning shear?
quiz.explanation: Sharpening restores the shearâs cutting ability.

quiz.q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a dull one?
quiz.explanation: Less force means less chance of slipping.

quiz.q: What should you do before grafting a new tree?
quiz.explanation: Disinfecting prevents disease transmission.

quiz.q: What is a good source of free grafting supplies?
quiz.explanation: NGOs often distribute subsidised or free farm inputs.
